title: Variables & Types
subtitle: int, float, str, bool, None, and dynamic typing
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Programs need to store and work with data — names, numbers, prices, flags. Without variables, every value would be hardcoded.
whyItExists.solution: Variables are named containers for values. Python has built-in types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, and None. Python figures out the type automatically — you don't declare it.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every program uses variables. Understanding types prevents bugs like '2' + 2 (TypeError) vs 2 + 2 (4).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Python is dynamically typed — types are determined at runtime. For large projects, add type hints (Python 3.5+) for clarity and tooling support.

explainModes.beginner: A variable is like a labelled box. name = 'Prashant' puts the text 'Prashant' in a box called name. age = 28 puts the number 28 in a box called age. You can look at or change what's in the box at any time.
explainModes.simple: Python has 5 core types: int (42), float (3.14), str ('hello'), bool (True/False), None. Assign with =. Check type with type(). Convert with int(), float(), str(). Variables are dynamically typed — the same variable can hold different types at different times.
explainModes.standard: Python is dynamically and strongly typed. Dynamically typed: no type declaration needed, types are checked at runtime. Strongly typed: Python won't silently coerce — '2' + 2 is a TypeError. Variables are references to objects — assignment binds a name to an object in memory. Multiple assignment: a = b = c = 0. Tuple unpacking: x, y = 10, 20.
explainModes.technical: Every Python object has a type, an identity (id()), and a value. int is arbitrary-precision (no overflow). float uses IEEE 754 double precision. str is immutable Unicode. bool is a subclass of int (True == 1, False == 0). None is a singleton — the only instance of NoneType. is tests identity (same object), == tests equality (same value).
explainModes.deepDive: CPython interns small integers (-5 to 256) and short strings for performance — this is why id(a) == id(b) sometimes holds for small ints even without assignment. Python's type system uses protocols (duck typing) and abstract base classes. Type hints (PEP 484) are annotations only — Python doesn't enforce them at runtime (use mypy for static checking). Walrus operator (PEP 572): n := len(data) assigns and returns in an expression.

content.code:
# Assign a value to a variable
name = 'Prashant'
age = 28
height = 5.9
is_student = True
notes = None   # no value yet

# Print variables
print(name)    # Prashant
print(age)     # 28

# Multiple assignment
x = y = z = 0

# Tuple unpacking — assign multiple at once
lat, lon = 28.6, 77.2
print(lat, lon)  # 28.6 77.2

# Swap without a temp variable
a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)  # 20 10

# int — whole numbers (no size limit)
count = 42
big = 1_000_000   # underscores for readability
negative = -7

# float — decimal numbers (IEEE 754)
price = 9.99
pi = 3.14159

# str — text (single or double quotes, immutable)
greeting = 'Hello'
path = "C:/Users/prashant"
multiline = '''Line one
Line two'''

# bool — True or False (capital T and F!)
is_active = True
has_errors = False

# None — absence of value
result = None

# Check type
print(type(42))         # <class 'int'>
print(type(3.14))       # <class 'float'>
print(type('hello'))    # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))       # <class 'bool'>
print(type(None))       # <class 'NoneType'>

# Convert between types
num_str = '42'
num_int = int(num_str)    # '42' → 42
num_float = float('3.14') # '3.14' → 3.14
text = str(100)           # 100 → '100'
bool_val = bool(0)        # 0 → False
bool_val2 = bool('hello') # non-empty string → True

# input() always returns a string — convert it!
age_str = '25'         # pretend this came from input()
age_int = int(age_str)
print(age_int + 1)     # 26  (would fail without int())

# Falsy values (all evaluate to False in boolean context)
# 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, set(), None

questions.question: What is the result of type('42')?
questions.explanation: '42' (with quotes) is a string, not an integer. type('42') returns <class 'str'>. To get an integer, use int('42') which returns the integer 42.

questions.question: What will print(bool(0)) output?
questions.explanation: 0 is falsy in Python. bool(0) converts it to False. Other falsy values: 0.0, '', [], {}, None. Everything else is truthy.

faq.q: Do I need to declare the type of a variable in Python?
faq.a: No. Python is dynamically typed — you just write x = 42 and Python knows it's an int. You can optionally add type hints (x: int = 42) for documentation and tooling, but Python doesn't enforce them at runtime.

faq.q: What is the difference between = and ==?
faq.a: = is assignment (x = 5 stores 5 in x). == is comparison (x == 5 asks 'is x equal to 5?' and returns True or False). This is the same in most languages.
